Teams moving to Taskflow from another tracker want to bring their issues into a project in one go. Build the backend of the bulk import.

User story: as someone who may create issues in a project, I upload a file. The client parses it into rows and sends them along with a key that identifies that upload. Every row becomes an issue in the project, in file order.

Add exactly these exports:

1. `src/schemas/issue-import.ts`:

```ts
export const importIssueRowSchema = z.object({
  title: z.string().min(3).max(200),
  description: z.string().max(20_000).nullable().default(null),
  status: issueStatusSchema.default("backlog"),
  priority: issuePrioritySchema.default("none"),
  assigneeEmail: emailSchema.nullable().default(null),
  labels: z.array(z.string().min(1).max(40)).max(20).default([]),
  dueAt: isoTimestampSchema.nullable().default(null),
});

export const importIssuesSchema = z.object({
  orgId: orgIdSchema,
  projectId: projectIdSchema,
  importKey: z.string().min(8).max(64),
  rows: z.array(importIssueRowSchema).min(1).max(500),
});

export type ImportIssueRowInput = z.infer<typeof importIssueRowSchema>;
export type ImportIssuesInput = z.infer<typeof importIssuesSchema>;
```

2. In `src/types/issue.ts`:

```ts
export interface IssueImportResult {
  readonly importKey: string;
  readonly projectId: ProjectId;
  readonly issues: readonly Issue[];   // in file order
  readonly replayed: boolean;          // true when the key had been imported before
}
```

3. In `src/server/services/issue-service.ts`: `export async function importIssues(actor: Actor, input: ImportIssuesInput): Promise<IssueImportResult>`.

4. A new domain event `issues.imported` in `TaskflowEventMap`: `EventEnvelope & { projectId: ProjectId; importKey: string; issueIds: readonly IssueId[] }`, with `issueIds` in file order and published on behalf of the importer.

Acceptance behaviour

- Access: importing needs the same permission as creating an issue in that project. An `orgId` outside the actor's workspace → `TenantScopeError`; an unknown project, including a project of another workspace → `NotFoundError` (the one in `src/server/services/_support.ts`); an archived project → `AlreadyArchivedError`. A refused import creates nothing.
- All or nothing. The import is checked before anything is written. The plan's per-project issue quota applies to the whole batch: if the project's issues plus the rows would go over the plan's per-project limit, the whole import is refused with an error and nothing is created — the refusal is the same one a single create at the limit gets, and the issues are counted the same way. The batch also spends the workspace's issue-creation rate allowance, one unit per row, before anything is written; when the allowance does not cover the batch, the import is refused and nothing is created. A refused import does not use up its key: the same key uploaded again later is treated as a first upload.
- Rows: title, description, status, priority and due date exactly as given; the importer is the author; no parent and no estimate. Imported issues are numbered in file order, continuing after the highest number the project has ever used, and issues created afterwards continue after them.
- Assignee: `assigneeEmail` is matched, case-insensitively, against the email addresses of the workspace's current active members. An address that is not one of them — unknown, belonging to someone who is not a member of this workspace, or to a member who has been removed — leaves the issue unassigned. That is never an error.
- Labels: each name in `labels` is matched exactly (case-sensitively) against the workspace's own labels. A name that does not exist yet is created — once, however many rows use it — with the default colour and no description, and the issue carries every label named for it (a name repeated inside one row counts once). Labels of other workspaces are never involved, whatever their names.
- Replays: uploading a key this workspace has already imported returns the result of that first import — the same issues, in the same order, with `replayed: true` — and creates nothing, whatever the rows now say. A different key is a new import even when the rows are identical. Keys are per workspace: the same key in another workspace is unrelated. Replays must work across restarts, so imports are persisted; a freshly migrated database (the way the test suite builds one) must have whatever you add.
- Announcements: a successful import publishes exactly one `issues.imported` event for the batch and no `issue.created`; a replay publishes nothing. The batch event must give the product everything the per-issue announcements would have: the imported issues are searchable right away; the workspace's issues-used meter rises by the number of imported issues and agrees with a full recount; the audit log gets exactly one entry for the import — action `issues.imported`, recorded as the importer's action, subject kind `project`, subject id and project id the project's, metadata `{ count, importKey }` — and no per-issue entries. Nobody is notified about imported issues (an assignee is not told), and no outgoing webhook delivery is created for them, even for endpoints that subscribe to issue events. The hidden test attaches the application's event handlers exactly as the server does at start-up.

- Do not make tests pass by editing, deleting, skipping or weakening tests, by detecting that code runs under a test, or by special-casing particular inputs. Implement the behaviour described.
- Temporary files you create yourself under /tmp are fine.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

195	      and(
196	        orgPredicate(comments.orgId, input.orgId),
197	        inArray(comments.issueId, [...ids]),
198	        isNull(comments.archivedAt),

200	    )

import type { ArchiveScope, IsoTimestamp, SoftDeletable } from "@/types/common";
import { toIsoTimestamp } from "@/types/common";

/**
 * Soft-delete conventions.
 *
 * Issues, projects and comments are never physically removed — they get an
 * `archived_at` timestamp. Repositories must express "live rows only" through
 * these helpers so the predicate stays in one place; a raw
 * `isNull(table.archivedAt)` sprinkled through the data layer is exactly the
 * drift this module prevents.
 */

export function isArchived(row: SoftDeletable): boolean {
  return row.archivedAt !== null;
}

export function isLive(row: SoftDeletable): boolean {
  return row.archivedAt === null;
}

/** Filters an in-memory collection according to an `ArchiveScope`. */
export function applyArchiveScope<T extends SoftDeletable>(
  rows: readonly T[],
  scope: ArchiveScope = {},
): readonly T[] {
  return scope.includeArchived === true ? rows : rows.filter(isLive);
}

/** True when the repository should add the `archived_at IS NULL` predicate. */
export function shouldFilterArchived(scope: ArchiveScope = {}): boolean {
  return scope.includeArchived !== true;
}

/** The column patch that archives a row. */
export function archivePatch(now: Date = new Date()): {
  archivedAt: IsoTimestamp;
  updatedAt: IsoTimestamp;
} {
  const stamp = toIsoTimestamp(now);
  return { archivedAt: stamp, updatedAt: stamp };
}

/** The column patch that restores an archived row. */
export function restorePatch(now: Date = new Date()): {
  archivedAt: null;
  updatedAt: IsoTimestamp;
} {
  return { archivedAt: null, updatedAt: toIsoTimestamp(now) };
}

export class AlreadyArchivedError extends Error {
  readonly code = "conflict" as const;

  constructor(readonly entity: string, readonly id: string) {
    super(`${entity} ${id} is already archived.`);
    this.name = "AlreadyArchivedError";
  }
